facts.fact: Lifestyle creep describes spending rising to match income increases, which can leave savings rate flat even as pay grows.
facts.caveat: A behavioral pattern observed broadly, not a universal outcome.

facts.fact: Loss aversion (a well-documented behavioral economics finding) describes people generally feeling the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equivalent gain, which can distort spending and investing decisions.
facts.caveat: A general finding from behavioral economics research; individual reactions vary.

facts.fact: Research on financial behavior often points to emotional and habitual triggers (stress, boredom, social pressure), not just lack of information, as key drivers of overspending.
facts.caveat: General behavioral pattern; not a diagnosis of any individual's situation.

facts.fact: The sunk cost fallacy describes continuing to invest money/time into something because of what's already been spent, rather than its future value.
facts.caveat: A well-known cognitive bias; applies generally, not to every financial decision.

facts.fact: Automatic, 'set it and forget it' systems (auto-transfers, auto-investing) are commonly recommended in behavioral finance because they remove reliance on ongoing willpower.
facts.caveat: A widely cited behavioral design principle, not a guarantee of results.

facts.fact: Money attitudes are often shaped early by family/environment ('money scripts'), a concept used in financial therapy and coaching literature.
facts.caveat: A framework used in financial psychology literature, not a clinical diagnosis.
